Evening. You check your ticket, just out of habit. The first number matches. The second. The third.
You check again. And again. Your hands are shaking so hard you have to put the ticket down on the table.
You just won one hundred million dollars. The odds were one in two hundred ninety-two million.
In a week, you'll have more money than you could earn in ten lifetimes.
In a month, you'll have relatives you've never heard of.
And in a year, you'll learn what money really can't buy. And it's not what you think.
But first, rule number zero. Don't tell anyone.
That night, you can't sleep, so you make a list.
Quit your job. In style, with the speech you've been rehearsing for years.
A house by the ocean. The car you've only ever seen online. Pay off your parents' mortgage.
A trip around the world. The best restaurants. A watch that costs as much as an apartment.
A new phone every month. A personal chef. Front-row seats to any game.
And maybe something good: a school, an animal shelter, a foundation with your name on it.
You do the math. Even if you spend a million a year, the money will last a hundred years.
That's mistake number one. Because a hundred million on the ticket and a hundred million in the bank are two very different numbers.
Rule one: the number in the ad isn't the money.
One hundred million is an annuity. Thirty payments over twenty-nine years, each one five percent bigger than the last.
Want it all at once? Then you get less than half. About forty-five million.
Rule two: taxes. The lottery immediately withholds twenty-four percent for federal tax.
But with this much money, you're in the top bracket, thirty-seven percent. You'll pay the difference yourself in the spring.
Plus state tax, anywhere from zero to almost eleven percent, depending on where you bought the ticket.
Bottom line: out of one hundred million, you take home about twenty-eight. If you're lucky with your state.
Still a huge amount of money. But not a million a year for a hundred years.
Rule three: silence is worth more than anything.
In some states, a winner can stay anonymous. In others, your name will be in the news by tomorrow.
Smart winners start with boring things. They hire a lawyer. They hire a tax advisor. And they don't buy anything.
Lawyers also recommend one more thing: sign the ticket and put it in a safe deposit box until you decide what to do next.
You're too late. Your photo with a giant check spreads across the internet in one evening.
Three days later, you have four hundred new messages. An old classmate with a business idea. A second cousin who urgently needs surgery.
A stranger who says you owe him, because he bought a ticket at the same store.
You change your number. A week later, everyone has it again.
The first year goes by faster than you expected.
The house costs more than the listing said. Then there's property tax. Then security, insurance, a gardener, a pool nobody cleans.
You buy your friends cars. They love it. So do you. For the first two weeks.
You lend money. A little here, a little there. Almost none of it comes back.
A friend asks you to invest in his restaurant. You say yes, because saying no to a friend when you're this rich feels awkward.
There's a popular statistic: seventy percent of lottery winners go broke. It has no reliable source.
But there is a real study. Lottery winners in Florida, with prizes from fifty to one hundred fifty thousand dollars.
The researchers' conclusion: a big win didn't prevent bankruptcy. It postponed it.
Which brings us to the big question. Does money make you happier?
In Sweden, researchers surveyed more than three thousand lottery winners. Five, ten, even twenty years after they won.
The answer is surprising. Life satisfaction went up. And it stayed up, even twenty years later.
But happiness, what you feel on an ordinary Tuesday morning, barely changed.
Money takes away the fear of bills. But it doesn't make your mornings brighter.
Scientists call this hedonic adaptation. People get used to a new standard of living, and what thrilled you yesterday becomes normal today.
A new car is exciting for a month. Then it's just a car you sit in, stuck in the same traffic.
And you can feel it. You have everything, but Tuesday is still Tuesday.
And then comes the price they don't mention in the rules.
You no longer know who's around for you, and who's around for the money.
On a date, she asks what you do for a living. You lie, because the truth would ruin everything.
Old friends stop inviting you to the bar. It's awkward when you pay for everyone. And even more awkward when you don't.
Your relatives split into two groups: the ones who ask, and the ones who are hurt you didn't offer.
You catch yourself testing people: would they still call if you stopped paying?
You built a fence around your house. And then you noticed the same fence had grown around you.
A couple of years later, you finally do what you should have done that first night.
You put the money into a boring fund that simply grows with the economy. You pay yourself a modest, predictable amount each year.
There's a simple rule of thumb in finance: if you spend about four percent a year, your money will most likely last for decades.
On twenty-eight million, that's more than a million a year. No yachts, but it lasts.
You go back to work. Not for the money, but because without something to do, the days blur into one.
And you notice something strange. The most valuable thing you won wasn't the house or the car. It was the freedom to say no.
And now, a question for you. The odds of winning the jackpot are one in two hundred ninety-two million.
The odds that you have a hundred dollars you could set aside this month are a lot better.
What would you do with the jackpot? And what will you do with that hundred?
Tell us in the comments. This isn't financial advice, it's a thought experiment.
There's a separate chapter in this story: scammers. To them, you're now the brightest target in town.
First come the emails: you've won another prize, all you have to do is pay the fee.
By now you understand the main thing: a real prize never asks you to pay for it.
Then comes a call, supposedly from the IRS: send money right now, or you'll be arrested. The real IRS doesn't call with threats, and it never asks to be paid in gift cards.
The most dangerous ones show up in person. A confident advisor in an expensive suit promises a guaranteed thirty percent a year.
Remember a simple rule: if someone guarantees high returns with no risk, they're not selling returns. They're selling a fairy tale.
Even a relative with a sure thing can be honestly wrong. A con artist and an unlucky optimist look exactly the same until the money is gone.
You make yourself a law: no decision on the same day you hear about it. Lawyer first, then sleep, then an answer.
And you notice that half of the urgent requests simply disappear once people realize you won't answer right away.
But there are other stories too. Quiet ones that never make the news.
The winners who end up fine are surprisingly alike. For years, they live almost exactly the way they did before.
First, they pay off their debts. Then they set aside enough to cover several years of normal life. Only after that do they think about buying things.
They decide in advance how much they'll give to family. One clear amount, one time, without endless negotiations at every family dinner.
They don't change friends, cities, or jobs in the first year. They put off big decisions for at least six months, until their head cools down.
They hire people who are paid a flat fee for advice, not a commission on a sale. That way the advisor has no reason to sell them things they don't need.
And most importantly: for them, money is a tool, not a new personality.
You look at your own life and realize you did almost everything backwards. But it's not too late.
